title: Walking With One
subtitle: Five sessions on discipling a single person the organic way, life on life, not a program
summary: Jesus could have started a movement with a crowd. Instead he took twelve men up a mountain and gave them years of his ordinary life before he ever sent them anywhere. That is the model this study recovers, discipleship as one person walking with one person, life on life, not a class you sign up for and finish. Five sessions trace the pattern. Jesus choosing a few instead of a mass. Presence coming before mission, the being with that is itself the training. Paul sharing not only the gospel but his own self. The way real formation happens in the cracks of a normal week, a meal, a drive, an honest hour, the way Jesus taught two men the whole of Scripture on a walk to Emmaus. And imitation over information, the sober truth that the person you are walking with is learning less from what you say than from watching how you live. It is written for two people at once, the one who wants to invest in a single person instead of running a program, and the person being invested in who wants to understand what they are in.
setting: Wherever your real life already happens, a kitchen, a car, a trail, a job site. The point is shared life, not a meeting.
forWho: Anyone who wants to invest deeply in one person instead of running a class, and the person being discipled who wants to understand what they are in.
rhythm: Five sessions, unhurried, one on one, spread over meals and walks rather than crammed into a slot.
leaderNote: Resist the pull to turn this into a curriculum you deliver. The content is your actual life, lived in front of one person. The five sessions are not lectures to perform but doorways into shared life, so read them ahead of time and then mostly put them down. Show, do not only tell. If you find yourself preparing a talk instead of planning a walk, you have already drifted from the model. The person is not your student in a seat. The person is your companion on a road.

sessions.title: Jesus Chose Twelve, Not a Crowd
sessions.bigIdea: Before Jesus sent anyone anywhere, he climbed a mountain and picked twelve names out of a following that numbered in the thousands. He did not build a program. He chose people, so that they might be with him first and be sent second.
sessions.open: Think of someone who shaped your faith more than any class or sermon ever did. What was it about being near them that a room full of information could never give you?
sessions.read: Read Mark 3:13-15 out loud, slowly. And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach and have authority to cast out demons.
observe: Out of a large crowd, how many did Jesus name and set apart? What does that number say about how he chose to change the world?
Notice the order of the two purposes named for the twelve. What comes first, being with him or being sent out?
talk: We tend to reach for scale, a bigger class, a wider audience, more people helped. Jesus reached for a handful. What do you actually lose when you spread yourself across a crowd instead of pouring into a few?

Twelve was small enough to share a life with and large enough to send. If you were going to give yourself to one person the way Jesus gave himself to twelve, who comes to mind, and what has kept you from starting?
Being chosen by name is a weighty thing. When has someone picked you out on purpose, and how did it change what you believed you could become?
sessions.practice: Name one person this week. Do not announce a program or schedule a course. Simply ask one person to share more life with you over the coming while, and tell them plainly you want to walk with them in the faith.
sessions.send: You do not need a crowd to obey this. You need one name and the willingness to begin.
sessions.passItOn: Tell the person you chose why you chose them, out loud. Being named is half the gift. Then ask them to keep an eye out for the one they will someday do this for.

sessions.title: With Him Before Sent Out
sessions.bigIdea: The training was not a curriculum. It was proximity. The twelve learned to do what Jesus did by being where Jesus was, and Jesus later told them the whole secret of fruit is to stay close, to abide, because apart from him they could do nothing.
sessions.open: Where did you learn your most durable skill, cooking, a trade, driving, from a manual or from standing next to someone who already knew? What did the nearness teach that words could not?
sessions.read: Read Mark 3:14. And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach. The being with comes before the sending. Then read John 15:4-5. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine. You are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
observe: In Mark, two things are named for the twelve, being with him and being sent. Which one is listed first, and how long do you think it lasted before the sending?
In John 15, what is the branch told to do, and what happens to it the moment it is cut off from the vine?
talk: We are quick to send people into service and slow to simply be with them. Where in your own life did you get sent before you were ready, handed a task before anyone walked with you?

Abiding is not a technique. It is staying near enough to draw life from the vine. In practical terms, what would it look like for the person you are walking with to be with you and with Christ before anyone hands them an assignment?
Fruit that lasts comes from connection, not strain. Where are you trying to produce fruit by effort right now, and what would change if you spent that energy staying close instead?
sessions.practice: This week, do not teach a lesson. Just be with the person you chose. Bring them into something you were already doing, an errand, a meal, a task, and let the being together be the whole point.
sessions.send: The work will come. First, be with them. That is not the delay before the training. That is the training.
sessions.passItOn: Ask the person you are walking with to notice one relationship where they could offer presence before pressure, and to start being with someone the way you are being with them.

sessions.title: Life on Life
sessions.bigIdea: Paul did not only hand over a message. He handed over himself. He told a young church he was ready to share not only the gospel but his own life, because they had become dear to him. The self was part of what he gave.
sessions.open: Who let you see the unpolished version of their faith, the doubts, the failures, the ordinary Tuesday, and not just the tidy public one? What did that honesty do for you?
sessions.read: Read 1 Thessalonians 2:8. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us. Two things are being shared here, the message and the man. Notice that Paul could not seem to give one without the other.
observe: Paul names two things he was ready to share. What are they, and why might the second one cost more than the first?
What is the reason Paul gives for sharing himself so freely? What had these people become to him?
talk: It is easier to give someone the right answers than to give them access to your actual life. Which one are you more comfortable offering, and why does the second one feel riskier?
Sharing your own self means letting someone see where you still struggle. What would you have to stop hiding for the person you are walking with to really learn from you?
Paul loved these people, and the love is what opened the door. Be honest, do you actually love the person you chose, or are you running a task? What would move it from project to affection?
sessions.practice: This week, share one true thing about your own walk with God that is not tidy, a place you are still growing, a prayer that has gone unanswered, a failure you learned from. Let the person see the real thing, not the finished version.
sessions.send: You are not delivering a product. You are handing someone your life. Give the real one.
sessions.passItOn: Tell the person you are walking with that the goal is not to collect what you know but to one day share their own life with someone the same way. Name that as the aim out loud.

sessions.title: The Ordinary Rhythm
sessions.bigIdea: The deepest teaching Jesus gave after the resurrection did not happen in a temple or a classroom. It happened on a seven mile walk to Emmaus, two discouraged people and a stranger opening the Scriptures step by step until their hearts burned. Discipleship lives in the cracks of a normal day.
sessions.open: Think back over the last month. When did your realest conversation about God happen, in a scheduled meeting, or in a car, a kitchen, a walk, a late honest hour?
sessions.read: Read Luke 24:13-32. Two of them were going that day to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened. While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. Later they said to each other, Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?
observe: Where does this whole conversation take place, and how long a walk was it? What does the setting say about where teaching can happen?
The two travelers only understood later what had been happening on the road. What had been burning in them while they walked, before they could name it?
talk: We assume real discipleship needs a room, a curriculum, and a block of time. Jesus used a walk. What ordinary slots in your week, a commute, a chore, a meal, could carry this instead if you stopped waiting for the perfect setting?

The best conversations rarely start on schedule. They arrive when you are already alongside someone doing something else. How could you get more shoulder to shoulder time with the person you are walking with, rather than more sit down meetings?

Jesus opened the Scriptures as they walked, not as a lecture but as a fire being lit. When has an unhurried conversation about the Bible done more in you than a formal study? What made the difference?
sessions.practice: This week, drop the meeting and take a walk, or a drive, or share a task. Put the Scripture into the ordinary motion of the day rather than into a special slot. Let the setting be normal life.
sessions.send: Stop waiting for the right room. The road to Emmaus was just a road, until Jesus walked it with them.
sessions.passItOn: Encourage the person you are walking with to name one ordinary rhythm of their own, a school run, a lunch break, a shared job, where they could someday walk someone else through the Scriptures the same way.

sessions.title: Imitation, Not Only Information
sessions.bigIdea: Paul did not tell people to merely learn from him. He told them to imitate him, and he sent Timothy to remind them of his ways, the how of his life and not only the what. You are not passing on a set of facts. You are the lesson.
sessions.open: Whose habits did you pick up without meaning to, the way they prayed, handled anger, treated a waiter, kept their word? How much of it came from watching rather than being told?
sessions.read: Read 1 Corinthians 4:16-17. I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church. Then read Philippians 4:9. What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
observe: Paul lists four ways his readers took in the faith in Philippians 4:9. Two of them are about hearing and two are about seeing. Why would he include what they saw and not only what they heard?
Paul sent Timothy to remind them of his ways, not only his words. What is the difference between teaching someone your ideas and showing them your ways?
talk: To say imitate me is either courage or arrogance, and Paul meant it as a sober responsibility. Could you say to the person you are walking with, watch how I actually live and copy it? What in your life makes you flinch at that sentence?

The parts of you worth copying and the parts that are not are both being watched. Since imitation happens whether you intend it or not, what one habit do you most want the person to catch from you, and what one do you hope they do not?

Paul anchored his imitate me to imitate Christ, so it was never about him being the point. How do you keep pointing past yourself to Jesus while still letting someone learn the faith by watching you live it?
sessions.practice: This week, let the person see you do one thing you have only talked about, pray with them out loud, ask forgiveness where you were wrong, serve someone quietly with them beside you. Show the how, not only the what.
sessions.send: They will copy what they see long after they forget what you said. Live this week as the lesson, because you already are one.
sessions.passItOn: This is the point of the whole study. Tell the person you are walking with, plainly, that the aim is for them to become someone who can say to another person, watch how I live, and follow me as I follow Christ. Then help them pick their one.
